content.question: When running the app from Android Studio, which button is clicked to launch it on an emulator?
content.explanation: To run the app and see it on the emulator, you click the Display (Run) button in Android Studio, which builds and launches the app.
hints: The instructor said 'click on display button'.
It triggers the build process first.
It is commonly represented by a play/run icon.

content.question: Why did Main Activity launch first on the emulator instead of the Login Screen?

options.text: Because Login Screen has no XML layout
Because Main Activity is first alphabetically
Because Main Activity has the intent-filter making it the launcher activity
Because Android always launches the last created activity

content.explanation: The AndroidManifest.xml file declares the intent-filter inside the Main Activity tag, which designates it as the launcher activity — the one that starts first when the app is opened.
hints: The answer lies in AndroidManifest.xml.
One activity has extra lines compared to others.
Look for the intent-filter element.

content.question: What is the AndroidManifest.xml file compared to in the course?
content.explanation: The instructor compared the AndroidManifest.xml to a blueprint of a building — just as a blueprint shows every section of a building clearly, the manifest shows everything about the app's structure.
hints: The analogy involves an engineer and a building.
A document that maps out all sections.
The word 'blueprint' was specifically used.

content.question: Where is the AndroidManifest.xml file located in Android Studio's project structure?

options.text: Inside the manifests folder at the top of the project

content.explanation: The AndroidManifest.xml is found by expanding the 'manifests' folder at the top of the project directory in Android Studio.
hints: You need to expand a folder at the top level.
The folder shares its name with the file's concept.
Look under 'manifests' in the file tree.

content.question: How many activities were present in the AndroidManifest.xml file in the project at this point?
content.explanation: The project had three screens — Login Screen, Main Activity, and Main Activity 2 — so the manifest file contained three activity entries.
hints: The number of activities matches the number of screens.
The screens were Login Screen, Main Activity, and Main Activity 2.
Count the screens: it's more than two.

content.question: What is the 'intent-filter' responsible for in the AndroidManifest.xml?

options.text: Securing the app with a password
Designating an activity as the launcher activity that opens first

content.explanation: The intent-filter element, when placed inside an activity's tag, marks that activity as the launcher activity — the one that opens when the user launches the app.
hints: It determines which screen appears first.
Removing it from Main Activity stopped Main Activity from launching first.
Only one activity can have it.

content.question: Can the intent-filter be applied to more than one activity in the manifest?

options.text: Yes, all activities can have it
No, it can only be applied to one activity
It depends on the Android version

content.explanation: The instructor stated clearly that the intent-filter can only be applied to one activity at a time. Applying it to multiple activities would cause a conflict.
hints: The instructor explicitly mentioned this rule.
There can only be one launcher activity.
Think about which screen opens first — it must be unique.

content.question: What is a 'launcher activity' in the context of Android development?

options.text: An activity used to launch other apps
The activity that is displayed first when the app is opened
An activity that handles background tasks
An activity responsible for database connections

content.explanation: The launcher activity is the activity — or screen — that appears first when the user opens the app.
hints: Think about the very first screen you see when opening an app.
The word 'launcher' relates to what opens first.
It is the entry point of the app.

content.question: How do you make the Login Screen the launcher activity instead of Main Activity?

options.text: Rename the Login Screen to Main Activity
Delete Main Activity from the project
Cut the intent-filter from Main Activity and paste it inside the Login Screen activity tag
Add a new intent-filter to Login Screen without removing the old one

content.explanation: To make Login Screen launch first, the intent-filter is cut (Ctrl+X / Cmd+X) from the Main Activity tag and pasted inside the Login Screen activity tag in AndroidManifest.xml.
hints: The intent-filter must be moved, not duplicated.
Ctrl+X or Cmd+X is used.
The destination is the Login Screen activity tag.

content.question: In the AndroidManifest.xml, where exactly must the intent-filter be placed within an activity's definition?

options.text: As an attribute inside the opening <activity> tag
As a child element inside the <activity> opening and closing tags

content.explanation: Unlike simple attributes that go inside the opening tag, intent-filter is a separate functionality and must be placed as a child element between the opening <activity> and closing </activity> tags.
hints: It is not an attribute — it is a separate element.
It goes between the activity's opening and closing tags.
The instructor explained it belongs 'inside' the activity.

content.question: Does Android Studio automatically save files as you type, or do you need to manually save?

options.text: You must press Ctrl+S / Cmd+S after every change
Files are saved automatically in real time as you type
You must save before running the app
Files are only saved when you close the project

content.explanation: The instructor explicitly mentioned that there is no need to press Ctrl+S or Cmd+S — Android Studio saves your files automatically in real time.
hints: The instructor said 'there is no need to save'.
Changes are persisted immediately without user action.
Real-time auto-save is a feature of Android Studio.

content.question: What tool in Android Studio is used to identify the cause of an app crash?
content.explanation: Logcat is the tool in Android Studio used to identify why an app crashed. It shows logs, errors, and system messages generated by the device or emulator.
hints: It displays logs and error messages.
Its icon is available at the bottom-left area of Android Studio.
The instructor said to use it when the app crashes.

content.question: What keyword should you search for in Logcat to find the exact error causing the app crash?
content.explanation: The instructor instructed students to search for 'FATAL EXCEPTION' in Logcat whenever the app crashes. This keyword helps locate the exact error in the logs.
hints: It is a two-word phrase.
The first word means deadly or severe.
The second word means runtime error.

content.question: What does 'Shutting down VM' mean in the Logcat output?

options.text: The physical device is powering off
The virtual machine (emulator) has stopped due to an error
The app was closed by the user

content.explanation: 'Shutting down VM' in Logcat means the virtual machine — i.e., the emulator — has stopped because an error occurred during execution.
hints: VM stands for Virtual Machine.
It indicates something went wrong before the app could continue.
The emulator stops, not the physical computer.

content.question: What does 'Caused by' in Logcat indicate?

options.text: The root reason behind the app crash
A list of all active activities

content.explanation: The 'Caused by' section in Logcat identifies the root cause of the crash — the specific error and the file or line where it originated.
hints: Causation implies reason or origin.
It appears after FATAL EXCEPTION.
It tells you exactly what went wrong.

content.question: What type of exception was mentioned in the Logcat 'Caused by' section during the crash?
content.explanation: The Logcat showed a NullPointerException in the 'Caused by' section. The instructor mentioned they will explain this exception in detail later.
hints: It involves a 'null' value being used unexpectedly.
It is one of the most common Java/Kotlin exceptions.
The first word is 'Null'.

content.question: In Logcat, how can you tell which files are user-created versus Android Studio's internal files?

options.text: User files are shown in red and internal files in blue
Internal files like ViewCompat are not visible in the kotlin+java folder; user-created files are
Internal files have a lock icon next to them
User files always appear at the top of the Logcat

content.explanation: Internal Android files like ViewCompat are not visible in the kotlin+java folder. You can only create errors in files you created, so look for your own file names (e.g., LoginScreen) in the Logcat trace.
hints: You cannot make mistakes in files you did not create.
ViewCompat is one example of an internal file.
Looking at the file names helps narrow down the source.

content.question: What does colon followed by a number (e.g., ':14') mean after a file name in a Logcat error trace?

options.text: The version number of the file
The line number in the file where the error occurred
The number of errors in that file

content.explanation: In Logcat, 'LoginScreen.kt:14' means the error is at line 14 of the LoginScreen.kt file. Clicking on it takes you directly to that line.
hints: It helps you navigate directly to the problem.
Clicking on it jumps to a specific position in the file.
It is a line reference.

content.question: How do you navigate directly to the error location in code from the Logcat window?

options.text: Manually open the file and scroll to the line number
Click on the blue file name link in the Logcat trace
Use Ctrl+F to search for the error in all files

content.explanation: Clicking on the blue file name link shown in the Logcat error trace (e.g., LoginScreen.kt:14) takes you directly to the exact line in the file where the error occurred.
hints: File names in Logcat are displayed in blue.
It is a single click action.
The link opens the file and jumps to the correct line.

content.question: What attribute must be set to 'true' in the Login Screen activity definition after adding the intent-filter?
content.explanation: After adding the intent-filter to the Login Screen activity, Android Studio requires 'android:exported' to be set to 'true'. Without it, there is a compile error.
hints: The instructor got an error and had to fix this attribute.
It means the activity is accessible from outside the app.
Its value must be 'true' when the activity has an intent-filter.
